title: Primary Function
learningObjectives: Explain the structural function of the vertical support tube.
student: State the primary structural function of the vertical projector-support tube.
instructor: The tube suspends the projector and mounting hardware and transfers their vertical service weight to the ceiling attachment.

title: External Load
learningObjectives: Identify the principal normal-service load and its direction.
student: Identify the principal external load acting on the projector mounting system during normal service and state its direction.
instructor: The principal load is the combined weight of the projector and mounting hardware. It acts vertically downward.

title: Support and Boundary Condition
student: Identify the ceiling support and explain how the vertical tube is restrained in the simplified model.
instructor: The upper end is attached to a ceiling support idealized as rigid. It prevents axial translation of the tube's upper end and supplies the upward reaction that balances the suspended weight.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the force transfer through the system.
student: Trace the load path from the projector through the mounting bracket and vertical tube to the ceiling.
instructor: The projector weight enters the mounting bracket, transfers into the lower end of the vertical tube, travels upward as axial tension, and transfers through the ceiling attachment into the building structure.

title: Critical Mechanical Response
student: Identify the dominant internal resultant in the vertical support tube for the centered loading case.
instructor: The dominant internal resultant is an axial tensile force. The assigned weight acts concentrically, so the base model does not introduce bending or transverse shear.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify parameters governing stress and elongation.
student: Identify the quantities needed to evaluate axial stress and elongation: tube dimensions, cross-sectional area, member length, elastic modulus, yield strength, and required factor of safety.
instructor: The required quantities are the mass and gravitational acceleration for the load; outside diameter and wall thickness for area; tube length and elastic modulus for elongation; and yield strength and required factor of safety for the strength assessment.

title: Expected Deformation
learningObjectives: Predict the sign of axial deformation.
student: Before calculating, predict whether the tube becomes longer or shorter under the projector load and explain why.
instructor: The tube becomes slightly longer because the suspended load places it in axial tension.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a centered axial-member model and free-body diagram.
student:
Replace the real mounting assembly with a vertical hollow circular tube fixed or supported at the ceiling and carrying the combined projector-and-mount weight W concentrically at its lower end. Include the member length and tube cross-section, and draw a free-body diagram.

STUDENT MODEL / FREE-BODY DIAGRAM SPACE
instructor: A suitable idealization shows a straight vertical hollow circular tube of length L, outside diameter D, and wall thickness t, attached to a rigid ceiling. The downward force W acts through the tube centroid at the lower end, and the ceiling supplies an equal upward axial reaction.
gradingNotes: The student need not reproduce the physical bracket. Credit a clear concentric axial-tension idealization and free-body diagram.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the axial model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real system into the simplified axial member.
instructor:
• The combined projector-and-mount weight is one downward force through the tube centroid.
  • The support is a straight, prismatic hollow circular tube carrying axial tension.
  • The ceiling attachment is sufficiently rigid.
  • The material is homogeneous and linear elastic, and deformation is small.
  • Local connection stresses are neglected.
  • Installation eccentricity, lateral loading, bending, compression, vibration, fatigue, and impact are outside the base problem.
  • The projector mass and extension-column geometry have published contextual bases; the accessory allowance, member length, material idealization, and required factor of safety are instructional inputs. No value is inferred from a photograph.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
student: Explain the calculation sequence before performing numerical work.
instructor:
1. Calculate W = mg.
  2. Use equilibrium to find axial force N.
  3. Find inside diameter and area.
  4. Calculate average stress σ = N/A.
  5. Calculate elongation δ = NL/(AE).
  6. Calculate the yield-based factor of safety.
  7. Use the required factor of safety to find the gross-tube axial capacity.
  8. Assess the result, distinguish it from complete-assembly capacity, and name a model limitation.

title: Axial Force
student: Use equilibrium to determine the axial force N in the vertical support tube and identify whether it is tension or compression.
instructor: Vertical equilibrium gives an upward ceiling reaction equal to W. A cut through the tube therefore gives N = {{projector_axial_force_N}} N in tension.

title: Hollow-Tube Area
learningObjectives: Calculate the inside diameter and annular area.
student: Determine the inside diameter and cross-sectional area of the hollow circular support.

title: Axial Normal Stress
student: Determine the average axial normal stress in the support tube.
instructor: σ = N/A = ({{projector_axial_force_N}} N)/({{projector_area_mm2}} mm2) = {{projector_stress_MPa}} MPa in tension.

title: Axial Elongation
student: Determine the axial elongation of the support tube under the service load.
instructor:
With E = {{projector_E_MPa}} N/mm2,

δ = NL/(AE) = [({{projector_axial_force_N}} N)({{projector_L_mm}} mm)]/[({{projector_area_mm2}} mm2)({{projector_E_MPa}} N/mm2)] = {{projector_elongation_mm}} mm.

title: Strength Factor of Safety
student: Determine the factor of safety against yielding and compare it with the required factor of safety.

title: Gross-Tube Axial Capacity
learningObjectives: Determine the strength-based gross-tube capacity and distinguish it from assembly capacity.
student: Using the required factor of safety, determine the maximum combined mass associated with the tube's gross axial-yield model. Explain why this calculated value is not the allowable capacity of the complete projector mounting assembly.
instructor:
σallow = Sy/nreq = {{projector_allowable_stress_MPa}} MPa.

Wmax = σallowA = {{projector_max_weight_N}} N, so the corresponding gross-tube mass is mmax = Wmax/g = {{projector_max_mass_kg}} kg.

This is only the idealized tube's axial-yield capacity under the assigned criterion. It is not a rated or allowable capacity for the complete assembly; anchorage, threads, brackets, ceiling structure, eccentricity, dynamics, manufacturer limits, and installation requirements may govern.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Assess the result within the model scope.
student: State whether the baseline tube satisfies the assigned axial-yield criterion, report its axial elongation and factor of safety, and identify one important effect omitted by the simplified model. Clearly distinguish the tube result from the allowable capacity of the complete mounting assembly.
instructor:
{{projector_engineering_assessment}}

Important omitted effects include anchorage and ceiling capacity, local connection stresses, installation eccentricity and associated bending, bracket stiffness, vibration, fatigue, impact, and manufacturer or code limits. This idealized calculation does not rate or certify a complete projector mounting assembly.
